en: Preface to Master Zhànrán’s *Kǎigǔ Lù* (Record of Lamenting Antiquity):
When a sovereign desires to unify the universe with all things, he must first establish the Dharma.

This Dharma is not merely intended to warn against the rebellious and arrogant, nor solely to intimidate the treacherous and perverse; it is truly meant to regulate the paths of the world’s intelligence, wisdom, and talent, and to constrain them.

The spirit of heroes and eminent men prevents their talent and strategy from being scattered or overflowing; thus, they are first able to focus single-mindedly on the practical application of governing the world.
Therefore, the Vinaya exists as the law, just as official ranks exist within a state.

When the law relaxes and instruction falls into ruin, it is not merely that one fails to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) or cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). It is a failure to realize...

Those who are fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the ten powers of supernatural knowledge (*abhijñā*) cannot be seen in this degenerate age.

As for those who seek to wear grass garments and eat wood, who cover their heads with a handful of thatch, and who sit facing a withered tree or an iron wall to sever themselves from the void—how can such people be seen in great numbers? In my own region, there was the Chan master Zhannen.
The Master was a banner of light in the southeast. His faculties were exceptionally sharp;

when meeting with those ready for the teaching, he was like a long sword leaning against the heavens—its edge meeting the target, cutting through instantly. Yet his school’s style was austere and cold, and his observance of the precepts was refined and strict.

He often lamented that in this degenerate age the Buddha-dharma was declining, and thus composed the *Kai gu lu* (One Scroll on Lamenting Antiquity), entrusting me with a preface. Having long been sustained by my late teacher...
Regarding the affinity between the needle and the mustard seed, I have often privately observed his forging and tempering.

Disciples of later generations frequently manifest great capacity and great function, wielding the "thunderbolt hand" and possessing both provisional and ultimate reality to sweep away all extreme views and stagnant interpretations like a flash of lightning; this is the earnest intent of this record.

This lies rather in the observance of the rules of sweeping, responding, and ritual propriety—left and right, square and circle. How could it be a matter of superiority based on the difference between the beginning and the end?
Generally speaking, the current malady of the Buddhist gate is that views and understandings float above the eyebrows and eyelashes, while intellectual sharpness is displayed between the teeth.
As for those who register their names under the disciples of Mozi and the Guest-Minister (Xunzi), they have relegated Gautama to the ancestral shrines.

Yet Nihui and Xudun abandoned their Buddhist chants to indulge in the "Feng" and "Sao" poems. Even those of lower status among them personally engaged in such tasks as sharpening tools or selling grain porridge.
They would slaughter fresh meat, cook fatty cuts, and cultivate glutinous millet to brew wine, until the savory flavors filled the kitchens of the Sanghārāma.

Occasionally, one might knock at the door and enter, only to find the air reeking of alcohol wafting around the meditation mats; even after years had passed, they would not once inspect the green [vegetables].

The lion throne. Beyond that, with but a single gourd and a single hat, carrying his staff he wandered like a cloud; he paid homage at Potalaka, gazed upon Mount Emei, attained the realization of Qingyuan, and studied under Shaolin.
Having thus completed the affairs of his entire life, he ultimately did not even know what the "five aggregates," "six sense objects," "four dhyānas," or "eight liberations" were.
This is the reason for the composition of Master Zhan’s *Kai-gu-lu* (Record of Lamenting the Past). Master Zhan roused and revitalized...

The intent of the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*) is that their primary purpose lies in establishing administrative regulations and selecting abbots, while the systems for ordination and itinerant practice seem not to reside solely in the Vinaya.

Nevertheless, since the Vinaya and the precepts (*śīla*) are like the obverse and reverse of a coin, if one wishes to cause the diverse multitude within the Gate of Emptiness— who are as varied as the myriad phenomena—
to lower their heads and restrain their minds so that they may revere the three-footed code of the King of Emptiness, there is no alternative but to rely on the Vinaya.
How could this be so? This record is the golden fortress of the true Buddha-dharma and the precious raft for those lost on the path.
Long ago, when the Elder of the Valley (Huang Tingjian) replied to Pujue, he said: "The Dharma-realm of Wondrous Virtue does not admit even a single speck of dust;
the practice-gate of Samantabhadra does not lack even a single dharma. It is like a revolving wheel-treasury: who is it that turns it? Who is it that stops it? In a single thought..."

Ultimate truth and skillful wisdom are fully perfected. If one can contemplate in this way, one will immediately sever the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings and will possess all the practice-gates of Samantabhadra.

If one does not contemplate in this way, then even with eighty-four thousand precious eyes that penetrate the fifty-four thousand eight hundred scrolls, illuminating every single character, it is like looking at a water mill; in the end, what is it? It is merely constant [delusion].
"Born into the Immovable Bodhimanda, this very place shall serve as the site for Buddha-activity.

Pujue said with joy, "I now have sixty monastic disciples in summer retreat, and the Elder of the Valley (Huanglong) has turned this Dharma wheel for them. This will save the old man from immeasurable complications.
Now Master Zhan is unfolding the wondrous meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* together with the spiritual friends of the ten directions; let us try to express our admiration."
The ancient intent was to eradicate all superficial and frivolous views, so that one might, through a single moment of subtle penetration, grasp the truth of the Buddha prior to all else.
If this were achieved, then the hundred thousand verses of the sutras and the forty-eight chapters could all be subsumed within a single word;
thus, it would be fitting for those lacking such wisdom not to claim for themselves the merit of offerings as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Record of Lamenting Antiquity, by the Nameless Elder; transcribed with washed hands by the disciple Qi Chenghan.
Composed by the Nameless Elder.
On the full moon day of the final month of summer in the year Dingwei, an anonymous elder sighed deeply.

His disciples asked, "Master, why do you sigh? He replied, "The days of antiquity are far gone; the regulations of the monastic groves have been swept away entirely. The Sun of the Buddha is about to set, and the Jewel of the Sangha is nearly extinguished.
I fear that the calamities of the Three Wu reigns may arise from this very day. How could one not sigh? (2)
The third son said, "I venture to ask for a brief outline of it. The Nameless Elder said, "Sit, and I shall tell you.

In the past, our Śākyamuni Tathāgata, through difficult practices and asceticism over vast eons, accomplished the unprecedented Dharma and entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa, charging him to protect and uphold it.
It has been transmitted from generation to generation, serving as the eyes for humans and devas, and supporting all sentient beings."
O Āyuṣmat, that which is called the Tathāgata’s single great cause and condition for appearing in the world is precisely this alone; it was his original intention.
Therefore, at the time of entrusting the Dharma, the Tathāgata foretold the future difficulties of the Dharma and commanded those who receive the Dharma to make a vow to uphold it steadfastly.

"Do not let [the lineage] be severed. Venerable Siṃha, knowing that past karma cannot be evaded at will, yet fearing that the Dharma could have no one to whom it was entrusted, sought out a successor in advance and instructed him to go to another country before he met his end.
Master Bodhidharma received the entrustment of Prajñā and came by sea, causing the Six Pāramitās to suffer poison; this is what is meant by "two."
The Patriarch said, "When I first came here, I frequently encountered poisonous drugs; I once tested them myself, and the rocks split apart because of them.

Now that I have found you to whom to transmit and entrust [the Dharma], my task is complete. I shall no longer provide further rescue. He then bestowed the robe and the Dharma, saying, "Internally, I transmit the Dharma-seal to accord with and verify the mind;
externally, I entrust the *kāṣāya* to establish the fundamental principle. In future generations, when the world becomes decadent and thin, those who doubt the precepts will compete."
Huineng said, "I am a man from the Western Heaven; you are a son of this land. By what means did you obtain the Dharma? What do you take as proof?
"You shall now receive this robe and the Dharma. Hereafter, it will be difficult for people to believe you. Simply produce this robe along with my verse of the Dharma to manifest your authority.

Once the transmission was completed, the Master suddenly passed away. Later, the Second Patriarch entrusted the Dharma to the Third Patriarch, saying: [The text continues with the account of the Third Patriarch’s succession.]

"Receive my instructions: you should dwell in the deep mountains; you must not yet go forth to transform others. A national calamity is about to arise, and I have karmic debts from the past that I must now repay.
You should remain in profound seclusion and wait for the time to come before going forth to transform others.

Observe the way the various patriarchs applied their minds—it can be said they were most earnest and most grave, never forgetting the Buddha’s entrustment. Later, Fengxue wept bitterly in the Dharma Hall. Great...
Yang Yao’s entrustment to Fushan was such that all deeply embodied the intent behind the transmission from the Patriarchs and Buddhas; it was by no means a mere formality.

Thus, from the Tang through the Song dynasties, dragon-like and elephant-like masters arose one after another. Yet nowadays, throughout the various quarters, people no longer speak of this matter at all.
Even among those who claim to be "good knowledge-holders" (shanzhishi), when one investigates the source of their transmission, they lack any definitive [understanding].
Relying on this, the wisdom-life of the Tathāgata will soon perish here; how can one not feel sorrow? It was asked:

"Since those who are good spiritual friends have received the grave trust of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, they ought to employ immeasurable skillful means and immeasurable patience to guide and receive disciples from the four quarters, causing students to draw near and attach themselves to them.
Thus, between predecessors and their disciples, the intimacy was like that of father and son. But now—"
He would frequently criticize and rebuke others; his own conduct was not upright, causing students to feel doubt and apprehension.

"The hearts of the ancients," [the interlocutor] said, "should not have been like this. [The Master] replied: "Truly, as you say, the Master-monks were indeed at fault. However, both the 'contrary' and the 'conforming' modes of conduct are rooted in ancient models.

Essentially, one must conform to the times of that era and act contrary to the standards of today. Why is this? At that time, the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) possessed roots of goodness that were fully matured. Their forbearance..."
It is easy to achieve discernment; it is like a fine horse that moves at the sight of its shadow. In these degenerate times, people are dull and stubborn;
if they are not sharply prodded, how could they be expected to act immediately? Thus, if frost and snow are not severe, there is no way to manifest the integrity of the pine and cypress;
if the whetstone is not hard, by what means can the edge of a sword be sharpened? For this reason, when the Great Being sought a verse from the rākṣasa, he did not worry about his consuming blood.
When the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) listened to the Dharma from Deva, did he loathe the man? He sought only his own benefit and took no account of the person.
Consider how the Second Patriarch stood in the snow until it reached his waist, yet the First Patriarch still rebuked him for his presumption;
or how Linji struck Huangbo three times, receiving sixty severe blows each time; or how Ciming visited Fenyang and heard nothing but insults and abuse; or how Ciming received Nanquan.
They uniformly revile and disparage [the laity]. Furthermore, they use wine and meat as "probing rods" and treat the killing of cats as a Buddhist ritual (*buddhakārya*).
At that time, those from prestigious families who passed the imperial examinations never once felt doubt or hesitation regarding this; they did not even study such things.
Consider this: when you speak of studying the Way, do you wish to manifest the virtue of the masters and monks, or do you wish to deliver yourself from birth and death?
If one studies merely to manifest the virtue of the teacher, the benefit truly accrues to another; what is the purpose of such study?
If one studies wishing to deliver oneself from birth and death, the benefit truly lies with oneself; why then blame the teacher or the monastic community?

Furthermore, since the beginningless kalpas, we have wandered through the six realms, lost and failing to return. Yet, when examining this closely, the sages and worthies who have transcended—compared to me—[are few].

You are immersed in worldly attachments. Though you exert yourself with diligence day and night, it does not compensate for even a fraction of what is required; how then can you find the leisure to reproach others?
Furthermore, those in the world who labor for hire and profit disregard both the abuse and insults before them and the whips and staves behind them;
they seek only to gain profit to support their own bodies. How could you, who wish to escape birth and death and attain immeasurable bliss, view others [in such a light]?
"Is it not the way of humanity to decline laborious toil? Furthermore, when parents desire their children to become literate, they engage a teacher, fearing only that the teacher might not be strict;
even when lashes and canes are applied daily, the child does not dare to complain.

How much more so for you, who seek the unsurpassed, wondrous Way—do you wish only for the master-monks to treat you with affection? He replied, "In antiquity, those who employed the 'contrary' method..."
This was established for the sake of one or two individuals of sharp faculties; it does not mean that it should be applied universally across all monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*).

If one were to apply it exclusively in such a restrictive manner, how could it accommodate a multitude of thousands? Therefore, we know that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the essential pivot for gathering the assembly, and it must not be discarded.
[The interlocutor] says: "You merely know that in ancient times there were thousands living together, yet you do not understand the nature of those thousands..."

The mind—in all cases, it is the mind that seeks the Way that constitutes the mind. Consider, for example, a rare treasure in the world: one who knows of it will travel no less than a thousand li to behold it;
otherwise, even at a distance of but a few inches, it cannot be seen. Is it that the treasure itself can distinguish between those who are close and those who are distant?
It is simply because of whether the person values it or not. Now, as for the student who desires to emerge [from the mundane],...
In the cycle of birth and death, nothing precedes the Way (*dharma*). As for that upon which the Way relies, nothing is more essential than a person of knowledge (*jñānin*).

Yet such a person of knowledge appears only once in an age. If one is fortunate enough to encounter such an appearance in the world, students will travel from as far as a thousand *li* to rely upon them, fearing only that they might not be accepted.
How could one dare to demand that the person of knowledge treat them with personal affection? In the past...
Zhe Fushan Yuan and Tianyi Huai were among a group of over seventy people who went together to study under Ye Xian Xing.
Upon seeing them, Xing immediately rebuked them, saying, "You fellows are monks who have already trampled through the prefectures and counties;

what are you doing here? Do I have any spare rice to feed such idlers as you? He shouted at them to leave. The assembly remained unmoved, so he proceeded to splash water on them. The assembly again...
He did not scatter it. Furthermore, when he sprinkled ashes over them, the crowd all became enraged and departed. Only Huaiyuan and the other two remained seated upright as before.
Xingsheng said, "They have all left; why do you not leave? Huaiyuan replied, "I have long admired the Master’s virtue and have come from more than a thousand li away.
How could I depart so hastily because of a ladle of water or a handful of ashes? Xingsheng said, "You..."

Since the two of you have truly entered the Buddha-dharma, there is currently a vacancy for the *dianzuo* (hall steward) here; could you take on this duty? Yuan said, "I, your disciple, am willing to do so.
Huai obtained permission to enter the hall. One day, while he was away on an errand, the assembly found the food too austere and plain, and they requested that a fine congee be prepared.
Huiyuan had prepared *liuhe* (six-harmony) congee. When the congee was ready, he went back to check on it and then went together with the others to the hall.

Once they had finished their meal, he summoned the administrative officers and asked, "Is there a donor who has provided a vegetarian feast today? They replied, "No. He asked again, "Has there been an offering of alms-clothing in the hall?

They replied, "No. "If this is so," he said, "then from where did this congee come? They said, "Let us ask the kitchen master (*diànzuò*). Thereupon, Huiyuan confessed, saying, "I saw that the assembly..."
Kudan said, "I have indeed done this myself. Xing-sheng said, "If you have such good intentions, there will be no time too late to do so when you become the abbot in the future.
Why must you privately steal property belonging to the monastery to curry favor? He ordered the administrators to appraise Yuan’s robes and bowl;
whatever their value was, it was all returned to the monastery's common fund, and Yuan was expelled from the community. Yuan pleaded with him repeatedly, but [he would not relent].
Xuefeng did not grant his request. Yuanzhou then sought permission from the Mountain Venerables and the lay patrons (*dānapati*), begging for them to allow him to register as a resident monk.
Xuefeng became enraged and said, "I told you that you were no good man! Do you wish to intimidate me with your status and position? Get out at once!

Yuanzhou replied, "If this is the case, I do not dare hope for formal registration. However, it would suffice if you would permit me to attend the Dharma assembly when you ascend the hall. Only then did Xuefeng relent.
He nodded in agreement. Yuan stayed in a corridor room at another temple at the foot of the mountain. One day, the Master went to see him and asked, "How long have you been living here?
He replied, "It has already been half a year. The Master said, "Have you paid the rent for this permanent residence? He replied, "No. The Master said, "This is a permanent residence.
How dare you occupy it by theft? You must return it immediately; otherwise, I shall report you to the authorities. Yuan then...
Hua gave it to him, and he lived separately within the city. Every time he visited him, [Hua] showed increasingly respectful demeanor.

Thereupon, the official returned to the mountain and informed the assembly, saying, "There is an ancient Buddha at Ye County; you all should know this. The assembly asked, "Who is this ancient Buddha?"
Master Xing said, "Yuan Gong was truly an ancient Buddha. The entire assembly was initially astonished; they prepared an abundance of incense and flowers and entered the city to welcome him back.

Master Xing specifically ascended the hall for him and transmitted the Buddha-dharma face-to-face. Since ancient times, Yuan alone has been the only one for whom the Dharma was transmitted within the Dharma Hall.
Furthermore, while Yuan served as the *diànzuò* (steward), he used the property of the monastery to provide for the monks of the monastery. Regarding this—

The principle is not lacking. Since the compensation for damages has already been excessive, why pursue him further? As for staying in a room at another temple, what does it have to do with the provincial administration?

If he does not return the rent, one may report him to the authorities and pursue him; for the provincial administration to intervene would be going too far. Yet Master Huiyuan ultimately did not move.
I observe his mind; it is truly like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, which cannot be moved by the eight winds.
That his fame spreads through ten thousand generations is entirely due to the realization achieved by the Duke (Xue Feng).

If people of the present day were to witness such a matter and the public discourse were to be in turmoil, where would there be any fragrant reputation like that of Master Huiyuan? Alas! As the distance from antiquity grows ever greater, how can I help but sigh?
Two or three of the disciples said, "This is indeed so. Yet, is this all that the old man laments? He replied, "Not yet.

I wish to enumerate them all, but I fear it would weary you to hear so much. For now, I shall speak of the most significant matters. Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Buddha-dharma came from the East;
at first, people did not believe in it. The Daoist masters of the Five Peaks vied with one another to create obstacles and established—"
An altar was established in the suburbs, where a fire ordeal was performed to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox; thereafter, the hearts of the people turned toward the true path.
Men and women who shaved their heads to become monks and nuns numbered nearly ten thousand, and the Baima Temple was founded to house them.
Thereafter, successive emperors and kings alike promoted this Way; indeed, there were no famous mountains or great monasteries that were not constructed by imperial decree. Its...
Those who serve as abbots are all renowned for their great virtue among the monastic community and have long been esteemed by the entire assembly.
Whether invited by an imperial decree from the Son of Heaven or recommended by high ministers, they may not occupy the abbotship without an official edict;

thus, there exist prohibitions against privately constructing temples or privately assuming the position of abbot. Among them, those who lead assemblies often number in the hundreds or thousands, yet they have never...
This is due to doubt. Nowadays, when monastic communities reach over a hundred members, they immediately claim to belong to the lineage of the "Red Lotus" or "White Lotus.

By treating them all as a single category for prohibition, the decline of our teaching has been brought about such that it can no longer be revived or rescued. As for the teachings of the Red Lotus and White Lotus:
"Originally, these were all laypeople; what business do they have with śramaṇas? The books they possess consist mostly of obscure and dark words that should not be known by others.
As for the scriptures of the Śākya clan, they were all translated by selected individuals under the auspices of the sage-kings of former dynasties and were decreed to be entered into the canon.
When śramaṇas lecture upon them, they must ascend the hall and take their seats so that the fourfold assembly may hear them together. This is entirely different from those who gather at night."
The private traditions passed down by the various schools differ vastly from one another, yet they are all equally prohibited;
is this not tragic? The teachings established by the Three Sages were fundamentally identical in their intent:

broadly, they sought to lead people to reform evil and embrace goodness, abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, cultivating themselves, regulating their households, governing their states, and bringing peace to the world; narrowly, they sought to lead people to rectitude.
With sincere heart and earnest intent, one breaks through existence to emerge into emptiness, thereby transcending birth and escaping death, realizing the fruit and attaining the Way;
all these are part of a single, unified principle. That unworthy persons appear in later generations—how could it be that the teachings of the Three Sages are not good?
It is simply because their spiritual dispositions (*gotra*) differ, and thus they cannot be transformed in the same way. Therefore it is said: "The son of Yao was unworthy, yet the son of Shun..."
Your son is likewise unworthy. If even the sages Shun and Yao could not transform their sons, how can one blame the followers of these three sages for having many who are unworthy?
Furthermore, from the fall of the Three Dynasties down to the present, have there ever been those who usurped the throne or plundered the state who did not study the books of the sages?
Yet we have never heard it said that Confucianism was abolished on this account.
He wrote this to condemn Confucius. Furthermore, those individuals were all royal ministers;
how could he have ever prohibited such people from holding office on that account? Among the śramaṇas today, there are certainly those who are unworthy, yet they have not reached such an extreme.
Moreover, among the ranks of śramaṇas, not a single person from such a class has ever been included. Why is this?
Has it ever been as urgent as this? Yet, the class of śramaṇas is vast and diverse; their dispositions cannot be made uniform.
It is not that the Buddha’s teaching is not good, but rather that the state’s administration of the teaching has not yet reached perfection.

Why is this? Furthermore, in former dynasties, the ordination of monks necessarily required examination; those who passed were granted certificates and permitted to shave their heads. In the present time, the ordination of monks...
Regarding the establishment of precedents for the payment of silver: since they are called "poor monks," how could they possibly afford to submit official petitions?
Yet, because Emperor Taizu granted them an exemption from these requirements, it enabled those of no standing to remain hidden. Consequently, such individuals fill the land.
Fortunately, there are teachers of virtue in the monastic communities who lecture on the teachings and discuss the Dharma, incidentally explaining the principles of cause and effect.
Through [the teachings on] sin and merit, hell and heaven, one’s mind is subdued, such that the distinction between the worthy and the ignorant, and between the good and the evil, may be discerned.
Thus, the worthy are seen in their dignified robes and caps, their deportment majestic; those who are unworthy all act in the opposite manner.

Now, if lectures and expositions are universally prohibited, not only will the worthy and the ignorant be impossible to distinguish, but it is further feared that the world will no longer be able to maintain its established order. Why?
Furthermore, those nameless individuals constantly claim there are things they have not heard of in the Way; yet you do not instruct them with the Buddha-dharma.
I do not know where you intend to place such people. As for this sort of person, they neither understand Confucian propriety nor are they conversant with the Buddha-dharma.
Having no home mountain to which they can be attached and no wife or children to bind them, if among them there should be those who follow deviant paths—
They respond at a single call; their devotion is like that of hawks and dogs, yet their wildness and defiance are like that of wolves and tigers.

Not knowing what time it is, one wonders what method could be used to bring them under control. Therefore, I say it is not that the Buddha-dharma is not good, but rather that the methods for governing it are not entirely perfect.
Furthermore, when the sage-kings of former generations saw a great monk, they would earnestly invite him to appear in the world, and five hundred people would sit beneath his seat.

Whether they be one hundred, one thousand, two thousand, or even three thousand living together, discussing the teachings day and night, they still cannot exhaust the Buddha’s profound and subtle mysteries, nor can they fully transform those who are stubborn and wayward.
Now, you wish to prohibit them from speaking [of these matters]. Are all people of this age endowed with the natural capacity of sages and worthies such that they need not study?
Or do you intend to allow their madness and perversity to run wild, deeming it unnecessary for them to learn?

Indeed. By this reasoning, those in power have completely prohibited the lecturing on sutras and the discussion of the Way, thereby providing support for those nameless crowds who are狂悖 (mad and rebellious) and 懶惰 (lazy), regarding such behavior as correct.
This is like turning one's spear against oneself and handing over the weapon to nurture their own evil.
How could this compare to establishing laws based on existing flaws to prevent them before they occur? In that way, our followers of Śākyamuni would receive far greater benefit. It was said:
As you have argued, the principle may indeed be appropriate; yet I do not yet know what regulations could be established that would be fitting and cause the Dharma to endure long in the world.
He replied: "I fear it is because we cannot find the right person—such as Fang Rong, Chu Suiliang, or Xu You.
If such a person were found, how difficult would it be to establish them? According to what has been established, there are no more than four types."

First, establish a fixed system for official ranks. Second, select the abbots. Third, institute examinations for ordination. Fourth, regulate itinerant travel. Regarding the establishment of official ranks:
it was like the ministers of military affairs in previous dynasties who, having received the gift of fiefs and lands, each maintained their own private retainers;

consequently, military power became dominant while civil authority grew weak, leading to the fragmentation of the empire. In our present dynasty, however, civil authority governs the military, and the flexible governs the rigid. It is not so here.
To receive such blame would it not be because the regulations were not appropriately established?

Emperor Taizu established eight officials for the Senglu Office, namely: Left and Right Shan-shi, Left and Right Chan-jiao, Left and Right Jue-yi, and Left and Right Ji-lu, as well as the Seng-gang and Seng-hui.
[He stipulated that] these must be those who thoroughly understand the Way and its learning, whose virtuous conduct is...
As for those who criticize [us], none are capable of this office. Alas, how can such a teaching of ultimate gentleness be constrained by the school of the Confucians?
It is like a sprouting tree situated beneath a massive rock; though it possesses the potential to reach the heavens, how could it ever fulfill its ambition?
Consequently, truly noble and eminent sages look down upon us as if we were mere trifles, casting us aside without a second glance, while the unworthy—

These individuals are merely commoners. Some offer silver to request ordination, while others rely on personal connections and favors; how could they possibly understand the principles of integrity, righteousness, probity, and shame?
I beg you to show compassion and instruct them in the proper models of conduct. Furthermore, how could they ever have mastered the Vinaya or the various vehicles of the teachings?

If there were a leader, and one hoped for him to govern those below, I do not know that such a thing would be possible. As the Book of Documents says: "If one is not correct oneself, yet desires to govern others..."
Such a thing has never occurred. Furthermore, the office of a prime minister must require a thorough understanding of the conditions of the people to be considered competent.
The court, in order to cultivate and nurture individuals of character, does not subject those of the Hanlin Academy to official inspections nor entrust them with administrative affairs.
How much more so for one like me, who dwells beyond the mundane world; to be constrained by petty human regulations would cause those who possess the Way to withdraw from society and remain unseen.

If one wishes to cause this Way to flourish once more, it is essential that the Sengluosi (Office for the Registration of Monks) be established as an independent office, no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the Zuosili (Left Office) or Youzili (Right Office).

Those possessing moral virtue must be examined and selected to preside over it; the Senggang (Monastic Officials) and Senghui (Monastic Councilors) shall lead its affairs, having been chosen through examinations based on their talent and virtue.
Furthermore, these offices must be administratively detached and not subject to the control of prefectures or counties. This is what is meant by "rectitude."
Only after establishing its foundation can one purify its source; thus, governing it will not be difficult. The position of abbot is a charge of morality and virtue, not a matter of mere expediency.
Therefore, in previous dynasties, abbots were invariably selected from among those of moral character and virtue in their region.

Local officials would recommend them, and the imperial court would issue an edict for their appointment. Alternatively, they might be renowned figures of the age who, by imperial decree, traveled to propagate the Way. It was because of this...
In the past, thousands and hundreds lived together, and people did not doubt this. Now it is otherwise:

possessing neither talent nor virtue, and having heard nothing of the Way or its study, yet being merely well-versed in worldly affairs, one is immediately named a *zhuchi* (abbot). This causes the monastic communities (*conglin*) to decline and the observance of ritual propriety to vanish from hearing.
Furthermore, when government officials fail to distinguish between the pure and the corrupt, they act impulsively with prohibitions, causing those who truly follow the Way to withdraw.

The physical body does not conform [to the Dharma], yet those who are unworthy employ a hundred schemes to scheme and plot. Consequently, the Buddha-Dharma declines further and the monastic communities become increasingly corrupt.

Furthermore, there are those of trivial character who do not understand the principles established by the Great Master; as soon as they have left the household life, they seek fame and reputation at all costs, taking this as their primary responsibility.
They rush headlong into the field of profit and fame, sometimes privately establishing mountain retreats or utilizing shrines and domestic altars.

Men and women dwell together; some occupy private civilian houses, making it impossible to maintain discipline or scrutiny. If one desires the communal living of hundreds or thousands as in ancient times, how could that ever be achieved?
Therefore, if one wishes for the flourishing of the Way of the Dharma, it must first depend upon the abbot (zhuchi).
If one obtains such a person, why worry that the Buddha-Dharma will not spread, that base people will not be reformed, or that worldly corruptions will not be driven out? [The text ends abruptly.]
This disorder is unjust. All unauthorized monastic establishments, as well as privately founded hermitages and temples where men and women reside together, must be strictly prohibited;
their abuses can be summarized by this. Regarding those who seek ordination through examination, they shall be ranked as right-hand śramaṇas.
Only those who pass the scriptural examinations shall be granted certificates and permitted to shave their heads; thus, the prevalence of corruption may be avoided.

Now, the Great Ancestor (Emperor Taizu) was about to confer the teachings of Chan and Yoga as two distinct gates: the Chan Gate conferred ordination as the means of deliverance, while the Ying Gate accepted registration documents as the means of deliverance.
From the Jiajing era until now, fifty years have passed; yet the ordination platform has not been opened, and those of the Chan school...
This current state is without any reliable basis; it is scattered in all directions, causing jade and stone to be burned together and gold and brass to be indistinguishable.
If one wishes to fully investigate these defects, then for all who have left the household life, ten summer retreats must be established as the limit.

Even if those of dull faculties cannot pass examinations, provided their virtuous conduct is verifiable, they must—regardless of whether they can read or write—be [recognized] by their preceptors and the community.
The mountain abbots shall provide a guarantee. For those of the upper grade, two taels of silver; for those of the superior grade, three taels; and for those of the lower grade, one tael.
They shall be sent forth by the Sangangsi (Buddhist Administrative Office). The Lusi (Vinaya Office) shall grant them tonsure certificates, though they are not permitted to take on disciples.

Regarding their studies, the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are established as the Three Learnings, with ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*) as the standard. They shall be admitted in succession for examination. Those capable of reciting the Vinaya...
He then took his original preceptor and, together with the elders of the various mountains, drew up a formal petition. They were granted certificates of ordination and tonsure.

For three years, officials from the Senglusi (Bureau of Monastic Records) were dispatched by the imperial court to tour and inspect the various provinces. They administered examinations at designated sites and evaluated the worthiness of the abbots of the various monasteries.
Those who passed the examination in all three sessions were selected and sent to the capital, where the officials of the Senglusi conducted further assessments.

I request that those who pass the re-examination be granted official posts to manage affairs. Their promotion or demotion based on merit and deficiency shall be conducted exactly as by the secular authorities.
If this is done, the wise and the foolish may be distinguished, corruption and confusion may be checked, talent may be obtained, and the Buddha-dharma may be stabilized.
Thus, there will be no idle people in the countryside and the state will have its regular revenues. Compared to the current prohibition against monks, how could this possibly be considered inferior?

Regarding the prohibition of traveling monks: in ancient times, because the nature of birth and death was not clearly understood, people traveled far across rivers and lakes to seek out spiritual teachers;
thus, they were known as "traveling monks" (*xingjiao*). Nowadays, it is not so. Some use the pretext of burning incense to travel through prefectures and counties, visiting famous mountains;
while this may resemble the practice of traveling monks, it is in fact far removed from the ancients. Nevertheless, as this has become a habitual custom, it cannot be prohibited.
Stop. Anyone wishing to travel far beyond a thousand *li* must obtain a travel permit (*zhìzhào*) from their local office; only then will they be permitted to depart for distant regions.
Otherwise, they shall be treated according to the regulations for unauthorized travel. For journeys within a thousand *li*, it is sufficient to present one's official certificate (*duòdì*).

When a traveler arrives at a monastic community (*cónglín*), they must be required to produce both the travel permit and the ordination certificate, and their names must be recorded in the registers for administrative convenience.
Investigation: Those who lack a license or a *duodie* (ordination certificate) shall not be permitted to remain.

If anyone is found to have been accepted through personal favoritism, they shall be investigated for their private conduct and private acceptance, and both shall be punished together. If one wishes to reside here, one must present the certificate to the Treasury Office before permission may be granted.
If one wishes to depart, the authorities shall verify that there are no transgressions and return the *duodie*. Only by following such procedures can one avoid incurring guilt.

Those who have fled and hidden themselves cannot be mixed in with the rest. If this is so, then compared to what is currently called the prohibition against wandering monks and Daoists, as well as those of obscure origins, [the present situation] is not even ten thousand times worse.
Thus, it is because the long-standing state of the world inevitably develops flaws;

to establish laws based on these flaws is the constant rule of the sages. Yet for customs to be nurtured until they become a prevailing wind is the great malady of all ages. Unless one reaches the ultimate...
I am deeply grieved by this degenerate age. If one carefully examines its source, how could it possibly achieve a pure transformation?

I observe that within the Confucian school, since the time of the Three Kings, there have been many instances of rebellion and deviation. These all stem from the fact that the sages and worthies of previous generations cut away and eliminated [the heterodox], and this has continued down to the present day.
Thus, the court regulations of successive dynasties each differ, and their increases and decreases are not constant; none of these are anything other than [the result of such historical pruning].

This is determined by the exigencies of the times. Take, for example, the single section concerning the recruitment of scholars: one first sought out the worthy and virtuous, and thereafter the *xiaolian* (filial and incorrupt);
from the *xiaolian*, one proceeded to the examination of poetry and prose; from poetry and prose, one arrived at literary composition.

Now, furthermore, the *shengyuan* (licensed students) are prohibited from entering prefectures or counties on their own initiative, and the *juren* (provincial graduates) are subject to the system of official inspection (*kaocha*). Suppose, for instance, that the current *shengyuan* were not...
If one examines and adopts [the former], its defects and harms will spread far and wide; neither gentlemen nor commoners will be able to restrain them.

Yet, literary composition is truly a field of learning that cannot be practiced indiscriminately; yet even here there is the corruption of favoritism and nepotism. How much more so for those of us who have left the household life—where one may become a monk this morning and be established as a *saṃgha* member by this evening.
How can such a transformation be made uniform? Therefore, I say that if one wishes to bring it to uniformity...
Transformation must be tested. Relying on these four principles, one does not constrain oneself through formal discipline, yet there is nothing that is not put into practice.
This is where the principle of "understanding without being told" resides.

It is said: "The ancients spoke of how, when the beard and hair fall to the ground, one transcends five hundred great kalpas; for this reason, even Śakra Devendra conceived a thirst for reverence, saying:
'He can cause me to be born during the True and Semblance Dharma periods of Śākyamuni Buddha and shave off my beard and hair.'"

Having received full ordination, he became a great bhikṣu. Even a woman such as Mātaṅgī, who had been a courtesan in her past lives and wore the *kāṣāya* robe only for the sake of entertainment, was still able to realize the fruits of the path.
If one were to judge by the standards of those you have ordained—where only one or two in ten pass the examinations—how could it ever be as widespread as it is now?
If it cannot be so, then you would be severing the roots of goodness in all people. This is...
"Could this possibly be the heart of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? [The Master] said: "I have heard that pearls and jade are considered treasures because they are rare in the world.
Since they are called the 'Sangha Jewel,' how could it be something easily attained by everyone? It is just like the honor of a golden seal and purple sash;
everyone knows these to be noble, yet how could one obtain them without a gentleman applying bitter resolve at a cold window?"
Indeed! If ordinary people were allowed to arbitrarily assume this status out of a desire for its glory, what distinction would there be between the gentleman and the commoner?
What difference would there be between the noble and the lowly? And who, then, would be willing to labor with ardent resolve at the cold window? Furthermore, as for the *xiucai* (scholar-official):

once he enters the school gate, he enjoys lifelong exemption from corvée labor, setting him apart from the common crowd. If he did not obtain this through examination, [how could such a privilege be justified?]
If this were so, who would not follow suit? If such imitation were permissible, then what role would the court have in nurturing talent?
I maintain that those with the natural endowments of sages and worthies are not easily found; it would be appropriate to allow them to gradually plant the roots of goodness.

However, it is not strictly necessary that they must shave their heads. Take, for instance, those in the Confucian tradition—how could they all be required to wear black silk caps before they are permitted to study?
Is this not a matter of writing? It must begin from childhood and only later achieve mastery through a state of non-mindfulness (*amūrcchita*).

I maintain that the station of the sages and worthies cannot be arrogantly usurped; therefore, one must examine and select with care. Furthermore, the former generation of śramaṇas was revered by kings and lords even more than the Sovereign himself.
If they were like those of the present day, what excellence would they have possessed to stand above kings and lords? As it has been said of old:
Regarding the entrustment of the Buddha-dharma to kings and ministers: how could this be intended solely to allow wicked people to harbor arrogance?
It is entirely intended to distinguish between the worthy and the foolish, establishing a plan for the eternal endurance of the Buddha-dharma.

Since the authorities have failed in this discernment, the errors of such indiscriminate practice have spread throughout the world, beyond the power of anyone to remedy. Why is this so? In ancient times...
Even when those who have undergone such examinations were tested for ordination as monks, there were still one or two cases that escaped the net.

Now, as there is generally no basis for verification, it is impossible to investigate them thoroughly. Consequently, there are those who become monks because their involvement in robbery has been exposed; those who become monks after escaping from prison;
those who become monks out of filial rebellion against their parents; or those who become monks due to domestic strife with their wives and children.
There are those who become monks because they have debts they cannot repay; those who become monks because they are distressed by a lack of food and clothing;

those who become monks because they wish to wear their hair bound up as a sign of devotion to Heaven; or those where the husband becomes a monk while the wife keeps her hair bound, which is called "practicing together" (*shuangxiu*).
Or there are cases where both husband and wife shave their heads and dwell together in a hermitage or temple, being referred to as "abbot" (*zhuchi*). Or...

There are those who dwell together with men and women they meet on the road; even among those involved in lewdness, theft, fraud, and deception, as well as artisans and craftsmen of every kind, there are monks.
Such individuals, having never undergone formal study, pay no heed to propriety, righteousness, integrity, or shame.
They merely put on a facade of being "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) before others, uttering great falsehoods—some claiming, for instance, that they have already attained realization.
The Buddha. Some claim, "I know the past and the future," yet they instead point to their teachers of worldly learning, calling this "verbal samādhi.
They fabricate claims of genuine cultivation to deceive both men and women, leading to further complications.

The government does not investigate the root of such matters, but instead suppresses them all indiscriminately. I say that one must not sever another's roots of goodness; I say that one must not cut them off.
The Buddha’s wisdom-life—how long it is! Suppose one were to pass the examination for ordination; then one would know how difficult it is to become a monk.
Not only do they each pursue their own Way, but they also vie with one another to admire its glory.

Those of sharp faculties read and practice day and night, while those of duller faculties give rise to a superior thirst and yearning. Are those who plant roots of goodness not indeed many? If it were not for study...
If [the distinction] is made heavy, then the worthy and the ignorant will not be distinguished, and the Buddha-dharma will be viewed with utter contempt.

This may be called the foolish gaining their advantage, while the wise exhaust themselves in sighs. The Book of Documents says: "The artisan who wishes to perfect his work must first sharpen his tools.
It also says that talent is rare; yet the sages have also said that all people can become Yao or Shun. On the path...
"A person can become a Yu. Furthermore, it is said: "The sigh that 'talent is rare'—is this not because the sages and worthies necessarily desire to obtain the right vessel?
If pearls and jade were as easy to obtain as tiles and rubble, how could they be considered precious or treasures?
You should reflect upon this. He replied: "Sages and worthies select vessels; they must not be appointed indiscriminately. There is indeed a principle at work here. Thus [it was said].
As the Sūtra says: "Do not store ambrosia in a defiled vessel. This is precisely what it means.

As for the previous statement that the office of abbot must be assumed only through an invitation from kings or nobles, this is likely not entirely accurate. Why? Take, for example, those from the Sixth Patriarch downward.
The likes of Mazu, Baizhang, Daowei, and Nanyue all lived as mountain hermits first, and only later were they recognized by emperors;
there is no record of any decree requiring them to take up residence in monasteries.

If one insists that a formal selection process must be followed to receive an official document (*tiē*) and assume the abbacy, then people will compete for reputation and true learning will surely perish. [The opponent] says: "You do not realize that the conditions of the times have changed."

Furthermore, consider those of antiquity: Fu Yue’s labor at the building site, Tai Gong’s fishing by the Wei River, Zhuge Liang’s reclining at Nanyang, and Zi Ling’s seclusion at Fuchun—none of them failed to harbor jade within while awaiting its sale.
Because there were those who possessed extraordinary treasures, [rulers] would not begrudge the dignity of their ten-thousand-chariot state to personally visit and recruit them. Now it is not so;

if emperors and kings do not venture beyond the palace gates, and if the worthy do not seek office by presenting themselves for examination, then the path of the sages and worthies will likely be severed.
Furthermore, in former times, when morality and virtue flourished, emperors looked up to and honored such men, frequently dispatching their close attendants [to invite them].

He traveled extensively through mountains and forests; whenever he encountered a venerable elder, he would invariably welcome him back to provide for his needs. Thus, there arose the tradition of the "inner dharma-hall.
Now, however, monks and nuns are not permitted to enter the imperial palace gates; how can this be compared to ancient times? Indeed, the responsibility of the abbot is no ordinary task;
it is truly the station for representing the Buddha’s transformation in the world. Since it is said that one represents the Buddha—
How could the position of the Patriarch be usurped by those who are merely ordinary? Furthermore, śramaṇas fill the world;
if one does not rely on a teacher of virtue and wisdom to take charge of this matter with vigor, how can their transformation of others be perfected?
Therefore, one must first awaken to great knowledge and vision, and possess its great functional power, before grasping the Vajra King’s precious sword and raising the Buddha-...
The Patriarch’s true mandate is to refine those among humans and devas so that the ancestral style does not fall into ruin;

this is what has been entrusted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and it is the heart of kings and ministers who protect the Dharma. Now, in this degenerate age of the Final Dharma, the true wind has fallen to the ground.
The distinctions between high and low have become confused and muddled, and the rites and righteousness of the monastic groves are no longer heard of. There are but one or two loads of rice...

These donors reside in small temples for a single *sangha* or three *sanghas*, where both parties remain in a state of confusion, wasting their years and months while merely being called "abbot" (*zhuchi*).
Therefore, I cannot help but lament over the past. Furthermore, I maintain that the abbot is the teacher of sages and worthies.
Now, the position of a teacher is not one to be spoken of lightly. As Mencius said: "The trouble lies in..."
Those who delight in being teachers for others are indeed great sages; yet even they spoke of the anxiety of serving as a teacher.
How much more so for one who is a teacher of both Heaven and humanity—how could such a position be usurped indiscriminately? Therefore, the Great Master of Tiantai also said:

"If I had not guided disciples and led a congregation, my station would have been at the level of the 'Purity of the Six Sense Organs'; because I led a congregation, I remained at only the level of the 'Five Ranks. Thus, I say of the teacher: [the responsibility is immense].

This position is not something that can be easily discussed. Furthermore, when parents raise their children, they exhaust themselves in toil and labor; yet, for the ritual of receiving them, one receives only four prostrations.
As for the ritual of serving a teacher, it requires nine prostrations—this may be called doubling and doubling again.

One does not know in what way the merit of a teacher surpasses that of one’s parents, such that the ritual toward him exceeds that toward them? It is simply because the parents... [only] bestow upon one life.

Nurturing the physical body benefits only this single lifetime; once the body perishes, consciousness is cast into another realm, and because neither side remembers the other, such relationships cannot form my *dharmakāya*.
Teachers and friends, however, bring benefit that truly spans vast eons.

Therefore, in the past, those who maintained the lineage never had a day go by without holding a *xiaocan* (small session), *yecan* (night session), *chahuà* (tea talk), *pǔshuō* (general discourse), *rùshì* (entering the room), or *shàngtáng* (ascending the hall). They guided their students, and their kindness was boundless.

Therefore it is said: "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who perfect me are my teachers and friends. Formerly, the Great Master of Fenyang did not deliver a *xiaochan* (informal evening discourse) for one night.
He saw a Hu monk arrive carrying a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), who urged him, saying, "There are six people in this assembly who possess the capacity for realization;
why do you not speak on the night discourse? Having finished speaking, he departed. The following day, the Master ascended the hall and said: "The Hu monk’s golden staff..."
Guang invited the Dharma to Fenyang, where six men became great vessels; he exhorted them to propagate [the teaching], whereby six individuals, including Ciming and Guquan, attained the Way.
Furthermore, when for one night he did not deliver a *xiaocan* (small session), the Holy Monk exhorted him, and he was guided daily thereafter.
Thus, how could his kindness and virtue not exceed those of his own parents? Therefore, when Xiangyan realized the Way, he paid homage from afar to Muzhou.
Mount [Shan] then said, "The great compassion of Master Miaoshan is an kindness bestowed upon my parents. Had he explained it for me back then, how could there be a 'today'?
From this perspective, one knows that the Master’s virtue was extraordinary. As stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:

"If there is anyone who can secretly explain even a single verse or a single phrase to another person, that person is an envoy of the Tathāgata and should be honored with the offerings due to the Tathāgata."
And they made offerings to them. Now it is not so. In various regions and monasteries, one rarely hears even a brief mention of ascending the hall for instruction.

Should there be one or two who engage in earnest deliberation, they do no more than rely on the sutras and secondary teachings. What follows these are merely worldly conventions, not worth listening to.
As for profound discourse and far-reaching talk that uproots the nails and extracts the wedges [of delusion], such is unheard of throughout the world. This is not right.
This means that I do not speak of it intentionally. This matter cannot be achieved without personal realization and personal awakening;

no one else can do it. Generally, many monasteries are presided over by those who are illiterate. Their leadership of disciples falls into three categories at most: the highest encourages them to perform meritorious deeds;
the next instructs them in administrative affairs; and the lowest merely associates with them as equals. Among these, the virtuous do not feel shame in serving those below them.
Question: When one studies the scriptures under a master, there may be an unvirtuous person who fears that his disciples will surpass him.
Upon seeing them practicing and studying, he says in anger, "You do not practice with sincerity; why study this as if you were pretending to be a great man?
He further asks, "What is the point of learning these mere verbal samādhis? Why not practice with sincerity instead? I venture to ask: what is meant by "sincerity"?
If one maintains their sincere resolve, yet there is no instruction or admonition, then the principle of being a teacher is not fulfilled. Why is this? A teacher is a model.
For example, there may be a good person in the world who initially cannot read or write, yet the deeds they perform are in accord with filial piety and fraternal duty.

Therefore it is said: "To be filial at home and fraternal abroad; to love the multitude universally and draw near to the virtuous—even if one says they have not studied, I must say that they have already studied.
If this is merely sufficient for self-benefit, how can one teach others? Suppose there were such a person:
Seeing that his conduct was upright and square, one might request him to instruct one's son. That person would surely decline, saying, "I do not know how to read;
how could I teach your son? This may be called being honest. However, if one lacks any knowledge oneself yet accepts disciples, this is truly a hollow pretense;
how can such a person be considered honest? In this case, even a single prostration would be deemed a misuse of the title.
If one cannot even accept two prostrations, how much less could one accept nine? Therefore, Huangbo said: "You fellows are nothing but wine-dregs eaters.
When I was traveling on pilgrimage, I saw a man beneath a patch of grass who still had a little breath left; I immediately filled my cloth bag with rice to provide for him."
"If it were as easy for people like you," Baizhang said, "then it would be a donkey-year before you even dream of it.

After a long silence, he asked, "Do you see any Chan masters in the land of the Great Tang? They replied, "In every quarter and at every monastery, there are those who lead assemblies and guide disciples;
are they not Chan masters? Baizhang said, "I do not say there are no Chan masters; I simply say there are no teachers. His meaning was that he did not say there were none.
Chan. One must be like Master Mazu’s single shout that left his disciple deaf for three days;

such a teacher of great capacity and great function is non-existent today—how lamentable! Not only are Chan and its teachers absent, but even those scholars who can "part the weeds to gaze at the wind" are few.
Why is this? For though there may be one or two who reach the presence of a teacher of knowledge, they never...

When there is a genuine effort to express [their realization], they will simply want someone to grant them a single "yes," at which point they will rejoice, considering themselves to have received certification (*pramāṇa*).

If one employs the skillful means of "pulling out the nails and extracting the wedges" to prune away what they value or shift their views, they will immediately claim that you are twisting them and will depart in a fit of anger. This is still considered the first rank.

Among those of heroic spirit and ambition, there is yet another class: having never heard the teachings of the religious tradition and having been a renunciant for but a short time, they immediately go to guard a mountain or sit in seclusion, claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) and deceiving and frightening people.

Furthermore, the venerable masters of old wandered on pilgrimage for years, becoming weary of the monastic centers until they themselves had attained some realization; only then did they go to guard a mountain.

Furthermore, while in seclusion, one nurtures the learning cultivated throughout one’s life. How could one who has merely left the household life, possessing no learning or insight whatsoever, presume to act with such audacity?
Take even the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, a most supreme sage; he still spoke of practicing through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
Entering samādhi, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra—whose rank borders that of the ultimate sages—still says, "May I always follow and learn from those of the three periods of time.
Those of antiquity necessarily relied upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), dwelling together with hundreds or thousands of them, investigating day and night, and mutually illuminating one another.
Even when they engage in mutual inquiry and response, they still find themselves at a loss. Let us set aside for a moment those who have not yet attained awakening;

consider instead those who, even after awakening, remain with a spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra) for ten or twenty years, deliberating upon the past and present and exhausting the nuances of all distinctions.

Their original master permits them to appear in the world if they are ready, or otherwise, they remain in lifelong seclusion. Yet, one does not know how those of the present day act, for they do not rely upon a spiritual teacher at all.

Furthermore, one does not dwell near a monastic grove. How could there be anyone who attains awakening on their own without study? Even if one were to awaken spontaneously, from whom would they seek certification?
From whom did they receive the Dharma? On what basis could they rely? If you claim that it does not depend upon a teacher’s lineage nor require certification, [how can this be so?]
Is it not the case that the people of the True and Semblance Dharma eras were no better than those today? Whom am I deceiving? Am I deceiving Heaven? Am I deceiving men?
I am merely deceiving myself. Alas! I did not expect such a flood of decline to reach this point.

Unless kings and great ministers rectify these collapsing threads of order, there is nothing that can save this world from its current decay. Therefore, those who hold office must necessarily be examined for their talent and virtue.
Only then can one hold the scale of judgment. Yet, there are those who still harbor doubts; for their sake, I shall further enumerate several points. Regarding what Master Huì asked:
Formerly, when Dōngshān Jiè was seven years old, he was studying the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*.
He turned toward his primary teacher and pinched his own face, saying, "The sūtra says there are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Yet I currently possess eyes and ears..."
[The Master asked,] "What of the nose and tongue? How can you say they do not exist? The teacher was startled and said, "I am not your teacher; you should go elsewhere to seek instruction.

Furthermore, when Great Master Yuanwu was reading the *Lotus Sūtra* and reached the passage concerning the stench of excrement and urine, he asked his own teacher, "How can excrement and urine appear in the text of the sūtra?
The teacher replied, "Your spiritual capacity is too sharp; you should travel extensively to seek instruction. Both men became eminent masters.

Nowadays, when a master-monk sees that a disciple possesses the potential for excellence, he immediately shuts his door to take him under his care, not permitting him even to move a step. Why is this?
He fears that the disciple might associate with good people and not remain attached to himself. Yet, if he desires for the disciple to become a perfected vessel, can such a thing ever be achieved?
Formerly, when Chan Master Guling returned from his travels, his original master ordered him to rub his back. As Guling stroked—
Baizhang said, "This is a fine Buddha hall, yet it is simply devoid of a Buddha. The Master then opened his eyes wide and stared at him.
Ling said, "Though the Buddha lacks spiritual power, he is at least able to emit light. While the Master was reciting the sutras, Ling composed a verse, saying:
"The world is so vast, yet you refuse to go; why do you pore over these old scrolls? The Master said, "I see that your speech is extraordinary. Ling had once...
"Who have you seen come? Ling replied, "I have seen Master Baizhang.

Thereupon, his own teacher gathered the great assembly and requested his disciple to ascend the seat. Ling immediately ascended the seat and declared: "The spiritual light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects;
though there are delusive conditions, these are themselves the Buddha of Suchness. At this, his teacher attained sudden and great enlightenment and prostrated himself in worship.
Qiyun said: "How unexpected it is that I, an old and decrepit man, have been able to hear this supreme teaching; one may truly call you a virtuous teacher.
Furthermore, Kumārajīva studied the Hīnayāna teachings under Udraka Rāmaputra in his youth, yet later Udraka studied the Mahāyāna teachings under Kumārajīva.
From this we know that teachers have no fixed status; each follows what they excel in. This is not like the fixed relationship between father and son."

Furthermore, it is impossible for a teacher to learn from a disciple. Setting aside the loss of prestige for a moment, even regarding matters of social standing, they are unwilling to study under such a person.
Why? Some say, "I am his teacher’s generation," or others say, "I am his master’s grandfather or great-uncle’s generation.
How could one possibly go back to him to learn? As for those who study, when they are questioned about their...
Regarding those who are superior, how can one even discuss their rank among peers? Mañjuśrī was not merely a descendant of Śākyamuni’s ninth-generation ancestor;

he still sat by the Buddha’s side and performed the rites of a disciple. Maitreya and the eight princes studied under the same teacher, Prabhāsa, and were thus truly the peers of Śākyamuni’s eighth generation.
How then could they be considered successors to Śākyamuni? Kāśyapa and Ānanda were brothers in the Dharma-gate; yet even Ānanda—
The Second Patriarch, Qingyuan Shitou, and others studied under the Sixth Patriarch together; yet Shitou became the successor of Qingyuan.
As for such sages and worthies, how could they ever have been separated by social rank? To take the Dharma as one’s teacher is a model that remains indelible for ten thousand ages.
Yet people today do not take the ancients as their standard.

The masters of old held aloft the ancestral seal and played with it with vital spontaneity; they employed the supreme mechanisms of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to provide instruction for sentient beings after their passing.
When students could not reach the point of inquiry, they urged them to maintain the practice day and night without regard for months or years, and only then would they enter into realization.
Today’s masters merely lecture on Chan according to the texts, engaging only in commentary and evaluation.
To chant [in this manner] is very much like a performer on a stage; though one originally intended to add a single stroke of a character, it could not be done.
Students fail to discern the black from the white; having heard it but once, they claim to have penetrated the essence.

If the essence were truly so easy, for what purpose did the ancients study and practice for twenty or thirty years? Is the faculty of people today sharper than that of the ancients? For this reason...
I submit: those who discourse on the "Essential Principle" (zong) today are truly possessed by demons.
Since ancient times, the disciples of the eighteen schools who categorized the teachings each excelled in their own school and all attained realization;
this is why their debates never ceased. As for the lecturers of today, there is no scripture they do not lecture upon, yet if one seeks their realization, I fear it may not yet have been attained.
However, in the monasteries of ancient times, whenever a venerable elder arrived from afar, the community would invariably prepare incense to welcome him,

strike the drum to ascend the hall, and earnestly request the essentials of the Dharma. Lately, however, among various quarters, those who serve as abbots fear that their teachers may surpass them, while the students...
I dare not act on my own authority. Such a standard of conduct has never been heard of in this world since time immemorial. Alas!
Those who left the household life in antiquity invariably maintained that before five summers of ordination, one must study the Vinaya;

only after five summers was it permissible to listen to the teachings and travel for pilgrimage. One would proceed from the status of an upāsaka to that of a śrāmaṇera, from a śrāmaṇera to that of a bhikṣu, and as a bhikṣu...
Only then is a bodhisattva not merely a name in vain; the sequence of their stages is all distinguished by their learning.
Yet now, as soon as one has left the household life, they shave their heads and receive the Bodhisattva precepts—this is called "direct reception.

They are entirely unacquainted with the fundamental principles of our school's tradition. Within two or three years, they claim to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), leading one another into deafness.
How lamentable! In antiquity, the position of the Head Seat (shouzuo) was the office of "holding the whisk" (bingfu). This was because the Abbot (tangtou) could not ascend the hall every day;

thus, the Head Seat would preach on his behalf, which is why it is called "holding the whisk. However, one must necessarily have realized the ground of enlightenment and have received formal certification (kexu) from the Master to serve the assembly.

After deliberating [on the candidate], he then serves tea to inform the assembly and clarifies his lineage of masters; only then does he take his seat to discuss ancient and modern precedents, expound upon profound mysteries, and examine the scholars.
Next in rank is the Hall Head (Dangtou), who is the current Head Seat (Shouzuo). There is no one who has not mastered at least one scripture.

He could not recognize a single character and had no authoritative lineage to rely upon. However, whenever several households provided offerings—whenever he could distinguish enough rice for several loads or provide for several halls of offerings—he would be invited to act as their teacher.
As for what he called "elucidating the profound depths" or "examining scholars," he dismissed these as trivial matters. To remain silent on all such things was his primary teaching method;
it was by no means that he did not speak, but rather that this was his way of engaging with the world. This is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Miscellaneous Remarks: It has never been the case that there have not been such people who style themselves "Teachers of Gods and Humans"—this is enough to provoke a laugh.
Those who left the household life in ancient times took birth and death as their primary urgency; they investigated day and night, striving with tireless diligence, never harboring any other thought.
If they did not attain awakening, they would continue for ten or twenty years without ever resting. This is why [the Buddha] spoke of the heterodox paths...

It is also said: "There is no leisure even to clip one's nails. Yet those who have left the household life today, as soon as they enter the Gate of Emptiness, immediately seek mastery and enjoy worldly benefits as if they were already accomplished.
They treat the reality of birth and death as mere idle talk. There are even those among them who, seeking to do what is "good," engage in the management of secular affairs.
He took the construction of monasteries as his primary task; compared to those who study for spiritual mastery, he seemed superior.
If one can ensure that cause and effect do not diverge, it is not as if there will be no karmic reward. Yet, when birth and death arrive, one fears it will be difficult to resist them.
In the past, the Great Master Yangqi assisted Ciming, personally overseeing the affairs of the monastery for ten years. By the time he resided at Yangqi, the halls and buildings...
The buildings were in a state of ruin. An attendant requested that he undertake the repairs, but Yangqi replied, "You all have not yet clarified the matter of life and death;
your footing is not yet firm. How could you have the leisure to attend to such secondary matters? He declined with this verse: Yangqi has newly settled in, the walls of the house are sparse;
The entire bed is strewn with snow-like pearls. I shrink my neck and sigh in secret darkness, Recalling the ancient man by the tree.
In recent times, the monastic communities have regarded this as an amusing anecdote, unaware that it actually serves as a fine model.
In antiquity, when emperors established Buddhist temples, they selected those with the Way to serve as abbots in order to propagate the state’s transformation. Now, however, it is not so;
when His Majesty constructs a temple at an expense of hundreds of thousands, he selects a youth to serve as abbot, calling this "substituting for cultivation."
What is meant by "substitution"? The Sūtra says: "I thought that the Tathāgata would bestow samādhi upon me, so that I need not labor in its cultivation;

yet now I know for the first time that body and mind can never substitute for one another. Furthermore, since the Tathāgata cannot bestow samādhi upon others, how could a youth possibly act as a substitute?"

If Your Majesty cultivates [the monastic order] in this manner, then those who recommend candidates will recklessly establish heterodox views and pointlessly deplete the state's fundamental resources, thereby failing the Sage’s heart.
How truly lamentable! Why is this so? For the office of abbot is equal in rank to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

it cannot be held by anyone who has not practiced with refined discipline and asceticism for twenty or thirty years and extensively refined their mastery of the *zongmen* (Dharma school). If a foolish youth were to serve as abbot...
It is not only that religious teachings have failed to flourish, but also that moral discipline has declined. As for the vast sums of wealth already expended, what further purpose can they serve?
From celestial beings down to humans, and even including insects, all suffer the pain of childlessness. Yet we frequently see śramaṇas exhorting others to leave the household life;
they never wish for them to be without children, but instead claim that the root of saṃsāra lies in craving and attachment. [They urge people] to renounce...
"Those who love renunciation shall attain liberation. Thus, a sutra says: "Bound by the ties of affection, one cannot part from love;

fathers and sons, each with their own sons, remain constantly entangled. To observe these words, they are exceedingly reasonable. Yet, [the worldly] do not realize that their own half-lives are not yet complete;
fearing the extinction of their lineage, they seek to continue it for ten or more generations. A child of ten years acts as a great-great-grandfather—how can this be compared [to true liberation]?

Those who exhort others cause mutual confusion and disorder among themselves; let us set aside those who are ignorant. Even those who act as Dharma masters are likewise like this—it is truly laughable.
Furthermore, Mencius said, "The trouble lies in being fond of acting as a teacher for others. How can one not feel shame when a mere child is called a "teacher"?
Judging these types of people by this standard, they are all the culprits Mencius spoke of.
The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "Kings do not bow; parents do not prostrate; ghosts and spirits do not show reverence.

If this is so, then those among the śramaṇas who tread the path that transcends the mundane and whose status is noble beyond that of gods and humans—why is it that in the present day, regardless of whether one is rich or poor, noble or lowly, or even a courtesan, a beggar woman, a great practitioner, or a layperson, as long as they have food and clothing to provide for them, they are bowed to?
To abandon one's parents and turn one's back on one's closest kin, disregarding shame and committing the sin of rebellion—this is the greatest of rebellions within the teachings of secular morality.
Within Buddhism, for what purpose should one sever such affection to leave the household life?

Regarding what is called "feeding the Sangha" (zhāisēng): when our Buddha was in the world, there was the practice of *piṇḍapāta* (alms-gathering). They would go out early to beg for food and return at noon to listen to the Dharma.
