It was because people of later generations were unable to endure this that the door of feeding the Sangha was opened, so as to allow practitioners to settle their minds in the Way and for donors to gradually plant the seeds of the *dānapāramitā*.
This provision was intended specifically for those who practice the Way.

This was indeed the case. Now, the śramaṇas of today are ignorant of the fundamental principles; they believe that those who provide rice for the monastic community do so solely for the sake of incense-burning and processions.
If this rice were instead used for expounding the sutras and practicing the Way, they fear it would cause a discrepancy in the law of cause and effect.
Such people truly do not understand what is meant by "cause and effect."

Generally speaking, those who have left the household life cultivate two matters: wisdom and merit. Wisdom consists of listening to the teachings, practicing Chan meditation, and extensively studying the scriptures.
Merit consists of performing manual labor with diligence and managing affairs to provide for the assembly.
Thus, even the Sixth Patriarch, a living Bodhisattva, still worked at the mill for eight months; and Danxia Tianran, though he had realized the Way, [still served as a firewood seller].
From the time he worked in the granary for three years until his establishment of the seat at Mt. Mui as the head cook for Xuefeng, Baizhang established the precept:

"If one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day. As for those of the present age who, upon first leaving the household life, immediately act like great men—never letting their hands touch water and sitting idly while consuming the offerings of the faithful—let that be for now;
I fear that all such practitioners of the Way are merely the "superiors" mentioned above.
Having received their offerings of blood and sweat, can you not feel shame?
Formerly, when the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, Lady Māyā descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

the Tathāgata emerged from his golden coffin to a height of seven *tāla* trees and preached the Dharma for his mother. His disciples asked: "The World-Honored One has already severed all worldly passions..."

[Question]: Regarding the passing into *nirvāṇa*, why was it that when gods and humans entreated him with such sorrow, he did not deign to look back even once? And why was it that when the Buddha’s mother arrived, he immediately emerged from his coffin to preach the Dharma for her?
[Answer]: It was because I [the Sixth Patriarch] was acting for the sake of the unfilial sentient beings of the末代 (final age).

Thus, the Sixth Patriarch left gold behind to support his mother; the Fifth Patriarch supported his mother at the mountain monastery; Muzhou wove sandals to provide for his parents; and Jingde carried his burden on his shoulder.
If one’s mother permits them to study, none will dare to turn their backs on their kin. Thus, the *Hokyōshō* states: "The Greatly Filial Śākyamuni Buddha spent kalpas repaying his parents' kindness.
Therefore, when those of the śramaṇa order abandon their kin to leave the household life, it is because the matter of birth and death is so great;
they do so out of utter necessity. This is no different from a Confucian scholar who leaves home to pursue learning; it is not a failure to be filial toward one's parents.
One strives for success so as to repay one's parents; likewise, the reason a śramaṇa renounces his kin is in the hope of attaining the Way to deliver them.
Thus, when Śākyamuni attained enlightenment, his parents and seventy thousand kinsmen were reborn in heaven. As the proverb says:

"If one son receives the imperial bounty, the whole family partakes of the heavenly provisions. Yet I find it inconceivable that those of our own generation would seek only their own ease and comfort.
They are merely pseudo-monastics. They lack entirely any thought of birth and death; how could they possess the mind that seeks the Way?
Without even ten years passing, several generations of their descendants will reach the end of their lives without once reflecting upon their parents. Is this the fault of our Teaching?
It lies truly with the people themselves.
In the past, Mahāprajāpatī was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Desiring to leave the household life, she sought ordination, but the Buddha did not grant her permission.
She then entreated Ānanda on her behalf, and Ānanda made the request. The Buddha said, "If women leave the household life, they will diminish my True Dharma by a thousand years.
Ānanda replied, "All sentient beings, down to the smallest crawling insect, possess Buddha-nature; how could it be that women alone lack it?"
"Yes. "If such women exist, why do you not allow them to go forth? When the non-Buddhists heard this, they thought, "The Buddha’s heart is not universal.
Thus they petitioned him repeatedly. The Buddha told Ānanda, "If those women can accept my Eight Rules of Respect, then they may go forth;
otherwise, they may not. As for the Eight Rules of Respect: even a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' standing, upon seeing..."
A newly ordained bhikṣu of twenty years’ standing should receive and pay homage to [senior monks].
A newly ordained bhikṣu of twenty years’ standing, upon seeing a bhikṣuṇī of one hundred years’ standing, should not receive her or pay her homage.

A bhikṣuṇī of one hundred years’ standing, upon seeing a newly ordained bhikṣu of twenty years’ standing, should offer him service and support. A newly ordained bhikṣu of twenty years’ standing, upon seeing a bhikṣu of one hundred years’ standing...
“Nuns should not perform offerings; this applies equally even to the recitation of faults and so forth. Ānanda received these instructions and taught them to Pāṭaliputrī.
Pāṭaliputrī expressed her wish to practice the Dharma of reverence. The Buddha said, “This will still reduce the True Dharma by five hundred years.”
Nowadays, there are many śramaṇas who live alongside women;
some even prostrate before women as their teachers, or allow women to occupy positions of seniority, openly receiving the salutations due to a śramaṇa without realizing at all that this is improper.
Is it not precisely this that is said to diminish the True Dharma?
Now, the teaching of the Buddha takes compassion as its primary principle and harmony as the basis for the community.
Therefore, those from all quarters dwell together, sharing a single peace with one another; even when residing among hundreds or thousands of people, they remain as one. Today, however, it is not so.
Should a teacher’s admonitions be too severe, or if their path and arguments do not accord, one immediately seeks to take one's own life to repay them.
Some compose anonymous leaflets or fabricate pseudonyms to distribute widely among officials and patrons, inciting them to harbor a lack of reverence and faith, thereby destroying the Triple Gem.
This causes both parties to suffer the retribution of the hells; it is truly lamentable. Why?

Because the Vinaya regulations do not fail to prescribe precepts against speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly or slandering the Triple Gem—all of which are subsumed under the ten *pārājika* offenses.
In Sanskrit, *pārājika* means "abandonment" (*parityāga*). One who commits this offense is permanently abandoned to the outer margins of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, it is called "abandonment.
Only the breaking of the harmony of the Saṃgha is subsumed under the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*).

If one reports that the offense has actually occurred to outsiders, it is what the Vinaya calls a "founded *pārājika*. If one reports to outsiders that the offense did not actually occur, it is—according to the Vinaya—[an unfounded *pārājika*].
This refers to what is called a groundless *pārājika* offense. Thus, one should know that whether the grounds are present or absent, both constitute the sin of slander.
This is why, during the new and full moon *poṣadha*, śrāmaṇeras are not permitted to eavesdrop;

it is because the Buddhas and Patriarchs feared that ignorant śrāmaṇeras might report [what they heard] to outsiders, and thus strictly prohibited it. Nowadays, however, this is not the case. Scholars from all quarters pride themselves on their own brilliance and—
Those who have ascended to the rank of the Dharma often fall into this error, thereby harming their own merit and fortune and receiving retribution in the three miserable realms;
all of this is due to not reading the precepts and the Vinaya.

Since the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, those who left the household life were treated by emperors as honored guests and were granted exemptions regarding living beings.

Externally, as the number of those who later entered the monastic order increased, it became impossible to discern their worthiness or folly; therefore, the precedent of "examination and ordination" (*shido*) was established, because those of sharp or dull faculties could not be fully accommodated by other means.

However, our Great Ancestor established a regulation outside of the examination and ordination system: that those who offered five taels of silver for admission would be exempt from [the examination] for the rest of their lives.
In former times, those who had renounced worldly service lived in transcendent leisure; the government treated them with the etiquette due to guests. Now it is not so.

Once one has received ordination, if one possesses fields, one must perform corvée labor; if one has dependents, one must provide corvée laborers. One must welcome officials and receive governors, pray for fine weather or request rain, and perform ritual assemblies and prostrations before spirit tablets—duties that exceed even those of a village headman.
Thus, while one desires to distance oneself from the burdens of secular life, one does not realize that one is instead increasing those very burdens. Furthermore...
Among the laity, for every village head or family patriarch of a hundred or a thousand members, all reside in a single household and are subject to no more than one tax obligation;

there are no double duties. This is not the case for the monastic community. Regardless of whether there are one or two, or even hundreds or thousands, it is required that every individual contribute.
Thus, it seems they are not as secure or exempt from burdens as the laity. Furthermore, when laypeople pay taxes on behalf of farmers, they receive exemptions; [the monks] do not. 終 (End)
Thus, they enter official service and establish households, yet they do not understand what the monks intend when they offer silver and submit themselves to the "shaven-headed" labor service.
If they delay and fail to pay, then the star-plaque notices will urgently press them with greater intensity than other types of labor service;
therefore, those in charge should investigate this matter in detail.

What the ancients called the "Fangzhang" (the Abbot’s quarters) was simply the position of the presiding abbot. Later abbots, being unable to preach the Dharma, would separately invite a Dharma Master to act as their representative on the seat.

Now, however, it has become a perversion to arbitrarily select those with worldly connections to occupy the Fangzhang, while the Dharma Master is relegated to what is called the Fayun Room; I do not know the origin of this practice. In ancient times...
There is no such thing as taking one's own copy of the meal roster. Later on, there were certain elderly seniors who had become thoroughly saturated with the monastic community;
they listened to the Dharma without weariness, regarding the master on the seat as their junior. Because there was no place for them within the hall, they would attend outside to share in the merit.

Even according to ancient regulations, this was already improper; how much more so for those who are newly entered and late learners to dare to imitate such excesses. What is the reason for this? It is because...
This refers to the extinction resulting from stealing the Dharma—is this not what is meant?

Those who practiced *zazen* in antiquity would carry provisions and rice for the journey, traveling no less than a thousand *li* to draw near to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). This was solely because they wished to inquire and seek instruction.
Yet those of the present day come to the hall without ever asking questions; they merely barge in recklessly, seeking only to dispel their delusions and confront their adversaries.
They disperse their resources for the sake of personal gain. In old age, they truly practice mindfulness of the Buddha, taking it as a mere topic of conversation.

Even after ten or twenty periods of retreat, they have never achieved any realization because their time was spent on such trivialities; yet they are immediately appointed as head seats (*śrāmaṇera*), leading later generations into deafness and blindness. This is the case throughout the entire world.
That no one is able to discipline them—is this not lamentable? Or is it not lamentable?
The governance of people by officials of the government lies in penal administration; the regulation of the community by śramaṇas lies in ritual and music.

Therefore, for all those who act contrary to the Dharma, they must be punished by prostrating before the incense burner, or even by being penalized with fasting; in extreme cases, they are expelled from the monastery.
In ancient times, one who was expelled was cast out by the community, and his name was equivalent to that of one who had committed a capital offense.

According to the Vinaya regulations, other bhikṣus were forbidden from sharing a lodging with one who had been expelled, as this would constitute a *pāyattika* offense. The expelled individual felt such shame that he did not dare stand before others. Now, however, the śramaṇas...
They regard the monastic groves as mere playgrounds and treat the rules and regulations as trivial matters. Entering and leaving at will, they refuse to accept any constraints;
they are like worldly people who have already incurred the death penalty, for whom judicial punishment can no longer be applied. Alas!
In ancient times, when donors invited monks for vegetarian feasts or ritual offerings (*zhao*), they would invariably select those of renowned virtue to prepare the incense and ceremonial implements.

They would prostrate and request them three times, and the śramaṇas would invariably decline three times before finally accepting. This was because it was said that their virtue was insufficient to receive the offerings and their Way was unable to save sentient beings.
In the present day, some śramaṇas recognize their own disciples as patrons, some seek letters of recommendation, and others employ ritual etiquette as a means of solicitation.
I ask: where does the doctrine of the "three refusals" originate?

In the monasteries of antiquity, whenever a man of national distinction entered a temple, the abbot would invariably ascend the hall to preach the Dharma, thereby consoling him for the journey from afar.
Such a tradition has now completely vanished from hearing.
In ancient times, when a donor’s family experienced a funeral, the monastics would go to offer condolences; they would invariably ascend the seat to preach the Dharma to assist the deceased.
Following this, they would recite the Buddha’s name at a distance from the coffin, and there was no custom of prostrating. Today’s śramaṇas do not comprehend these ancient regulations;
regardless of whether the mourners are male or female, old or young, they all go to perform prostrations. I do not know whether such conduct accords with propriety.
Now, as for the nature of a śramaṇa: a ruler cannot treat him as a subject, nor can a father treat him as a son.

The *Śīla-sūtra* contains the teaching that one does not prostrate before one's parents; if even toward those who have labored so tirelessly for us we are told not to prostrate, then what merit or kindness do these young men and women possess that they should all be bowed to indiscriminately? This is truly laughable.
In ancient times, śramaṇas were held in high esteem by emperors and sovereigns, such as when the Son of Heaven personally supported the skull of the loyal National Preceptor.
Yet, some who claim to emulate his example give rise to excessive arrogance;

therefore, great beings manifest compassion by performing humble deeds—whether by enduring impurities and shame, wearing tattered clothes and eating coarse food, or kneeling at palace steps to beg—in order to subdue those who are arrogant.
Each person knows their own lot. Nowadays, there are those who act as Dharma masters; they do not grasp the intent of the ancients but recklessly imitate them.
They don formal monastic robes and kneel on the streets to beg for money, while their disciples hold musical instruments to play along.

People do not consider this shameful, yet these men regard it as the fulfillment of their ambitions. I say this is not so. For the rank of a Dharma King is one revered by humans and devas; to kneel along the streets...
To beg is to bring disgrace upon one's dignity. For example, though a court official may be poor, how could there ever be reason for them to wander about begging?
Is this not what is meant by the ancient saying, "peddling the Tathāgata"?
The world refers to this as "Flaming Mouth" (Yan-kou), which is precisely the method of "correspondence" (xiang-ying). What is meant by "correspondence" is the strict observance of the three secrets:

the secret of speech through the recitation of mantras, the secret of hand through the binding of mudrās, and the secret of mind through visualization. Thus it has been transmitted from master to disciple by the ancients.
One must select a candidate whose conduct and realization are in accord and who is capable of receiving empowerment before transmitting it, as described in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-hṛdaya-vidhi*.
Now, who is one whose conduct and realization are in accord? It is simply this: a practitioner of visualization must sit in meditation and gather their tranquility.
Once the power of stillness is achieved, it flows forth from a single moment of tranquil mind—namely, transforming the great earth into...
To churn the great river into butter and curd with gold is no mere coincidence. Lately, junior practitioners have neither sat in meditation nor practiced contemplation;
they merely study the liturgical forms and have presumptuously ascended to this station. Not only will they fail to benefit living beings, [but they will also bring harm].
I still fear it may impair one's own merit; this must not remain unknown.

That ancient monasteries had "Recorders" (shuji) to document the facts of good and evil witnessed and heard at the time, as well as the essential Dharma teachings given by the Abbot to the assembly—just like the court historians—their title was not acquired in vain.
Nowadays, they merely transcribe and recite the commentaries on sutras.
This is all there is. Regarding the worthiness or unworthiness of those in the present age, and the traces of their good or evil deeds, nothing can be heard.
Alas! The Sūtra says, "Do not serve other devas," and it further says, "Offer no rites to ghosts and spirits. This is because one must choose upon whom to rely.

The Buddha feared that newly ordained śramaṇas would not know how to choose, and might instead support and serve those [other deities], thereby becoming their followers. For this reason, he requested...
There is a specific reason why it is not permitted for bhikṣus to enter the homes of non-Buddhists, butchers, or slaughterers. Yet, the śramaṇas of today disregard this entirely;
whether it be at shrines, celestial temples, or even private ancestral halls, they will go to dwell there as long as their food and clothing can be sufficiently provided.

They have no fear of the life to come, acting instead as partisans and kin to those [laypeople]. They merely say, "It is better to burn one's eyebrows than to let them fall into the fire," and so forth.
In truth, there is currently nothing amiss here.
Great Sages employ impartial transformation through unconditioned compassion; thus, the fourfold assembly beneath my seat has not diminished, with men and women coming and going as they please.
Now, those who hold power consider this to be an injury to social mores and a corruption of customs, and therefore do not permit entry.
To burn incense at a temple and listen to the Dharma seems not to have reached the root of the matter. Why is this?

Matters that wound the wind of propriety and ruin social customs mostly arise among one’s own neighbors and kin; through long-standing familiarity in coming and going, these are not the result of a single morning or evening.
How could such things occur in the midst of a vast assembly? Thus, the Book says: "Ten eyes look upon it; ten hands point to it."

How solemn this is! Furthermore, it is said that in a village of ten households, there will surely be those who are loyal and sincere. Whenever a sutra is preached, hundreds or thousands of people invariably gather together.
How could it be that among these hundreds or thousands there are not one or two who are loyal and sincere? Why would they willingly tolerate such things as these?
Throughout my entire life, of the matters I have heard that wound the wind of custom and ruin social mores, monks and Daoists account for not even one-tenth.
First: Laypeople constitute nine-tenths of the population. Is it because this is their natural lot and need not be prohibited?
Or is it because doing so would wound public morality and corrupt social customs? Or perhaps it is because they all burn incense and listen to the sutras that such things occur?
To blame others while neglecting one's own house is to fail to investigate the root cause.
In the past, great beings abandoned their entire bodies to seek a single half-verse; they constantly sold their hearts and livers to repay the Prajñāpāramitā;
King Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his body as an offering to the Dharma; and a Wheel-Turning King used his own body as a seat for the scriptures. Such was the sincerity with which they sought the Dharma.
As for you, when you see scholars in the capital listening to the sutras, they hope only for a single piece of cotton cloth; their initial intention is not even on the sutra itself. If...
Regarding those who have a karmic connection with the Dharma Master, each person distributes two or three bolts of cloth;
at the very least one bolt, though more is better and less is considered meager. When the Dharma Master appears in the world, his official recommendations act like talismans:
except for what cannot be obtained from the Sovereign, there is no place where they are not sought. Consequently, a single person may receive invitations from five or six different locations.
This is truly laughable.

Formerly, when Chan Master Huiman was by imperial decree residing at Hongji Temple, a nun from Zhenguo Temple entered and exited the palace precincts, acting with unrestrained arrogance and transgression.
Huiman immediately assembled the community to expel her. The nun appealed to the Crown Prince, who dispatched the Court Gentleman Du Zheng...

Lun attempted to resolve the matter of the exclusion, but Faman insisted on maintaining the rule and would not comply. The assembly feared that disaster might befall them, so they forcibly persuaded him to relent.

Later, the nun apologized for her transgression, yet Faman remained displeased. Furthermore, that nun was highly esteemed within the imperial palace; she was no ordinary person and could not be compared to others, yet even she was not permitted to overstep the bounds.
Now, as for this one Great Being (Mahāsattva), she possesses but slight worldly ties; toward those of the śramaṇa order, she should offer a hundredfold devotion.
I accept this. One does not know what constitutes shame.
Formerly, Dharma Master Zhizheng resided at Shengxiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan for twenty-eight years without engaging in worldly affairs.
Whenever he composed a work, his disciple Zhixian stood in attendance with paper and brush; as the words emerged, they were immediately transcribed, without ever [delay].

He was granted a seat. One day, his leg became lame and his mind grew distressed; he did not even realize he had collapsed. The Master still rebuked him, saying, "In the past, people stood on one foot for seven days.
You have barely managed to stand before you fall over. This is because your mind is frivolous. Alas!
Nowadays, when those who act as teachers and disciples are rebuked with a single word, they will not approach them again for the rest of their lives. How tragic!

What is called "sitting in meditation" (zazen) requires one to sever worldly affairs and establish oneself in a quiet dwelling, remaining as motionless as a corpse with breath—only then can one study the Way.
Therefore, those who studied the Way in antiquity mostly dwelt in mountain caves or slept beneath trees, eating wood-fruits and wearing grass garments;
the predecessors who practiced zazen all adhered to such simple vows. Lately, however, this pure tradition has undergone a great transformation, and people generally practice ostentation and luxury.
The head seat prepares the vegetarian feast (*bǎnzhāi*) before the assembly, yet the assembly also vies with one another in extravagance, making it impossible to restrain them.
Furthermore, those who study the Way value frugality and simplicity; with a mind at ease, they abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is why the World-Honored One renounced the glory of ten thousand chariots and went directly to the Snowy Mountains to eat pine and cypress. Was it that he had nothing to prepare? It was simply because for the sake of the Way, one must...
It is only through non-seeking that one attains it. Those who practice seated meditation today have no source of their own;
they solicit patrons and devote a year to their schemes, only to enjoy the fruits for three months. To exchange three months of enjoyment for a year’s labor is not a wise calculation.
Now, as for the Sangha, their primary duty is to continue the true lamp of the Buddha and to succeed to the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
Because those of antiquity did not receive the seal of approval from their predecessors, they did not dare to let their minds rest for the rest of their lives.

Thus, the Great Master Fenyang visited seventy-two spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) before finally meeting Shoushan; only then did he cease his formal practice, saying: "Ten thousand ages, the azure pool is a void realm."

It is like the moon: only after repeated stirring and searching can one finally recognize it; only then does one become its dharma heir and succeed to its original lineage. Among the venerable masters of antiquity, there were none who did not act in this manner.
To meagerly continue the true lamp, I have never entertained the notion of returning offerings [to my predecessors]. As for the śramaṇas of the present day...
Never having seen him as a true lamp, they turned to pay homage to him as their teacher.

Whether out of admiration for his empty reputation, reliance on his influence and path, pursuit of profit and sustenance, scheming for fields and houses, or because they had overheard rumors regarding their original teacher, they abandoned the old to follow the new and turned their homage to another.
To the former teacher, they became mere strangers, looked upon with indifference; yet they once claimed to have succeeded the Buddha’s wisdom-life—thus they changed their ways.
The Master said: "There are some who cling to their own ignorant views and consider those former masters who possessed no true knowledge to be their 'true teachers.
Those who sit in meditation or listen to the sutras are regarded as the head seat, the teacher, or the Dharma master; yet the teacher regards them as ordinary.
To investigate the reason for this, there is nothing else: they treat the true lamp of the Buddha’s life-essence of wisdom as a mere child's play, never realizing that..."
I know that this is of vital importance for transcending the world. Alas! I am weary; I shall rest. I will not speak with you further. Moreover, you, Master, are a sage.
Even when composing the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, you still said, "He who knows me is my friend; he who blames me is my enemy.
As for this book, what kind of person am I that I would dare to speak recklessly of the world’s successes and failures? Nevertheless, I wish to share this with you...
"In this present age, we must together uphold the True Dharma and maintain this great principle. If I am at fault, how would I dare refuse?

He asked: "Previously you said that both internal and external degrees were established by the Great Ancestor, and that they are most appropriate for the current time, as your teacher has discussed. Since then, the frontier provisions have been urgent, and the Imperial Court..."

When an official was dispatched to supervise the matter, everyone refused to comply, asking, "What can be done? He replied, "Those who wish to derive benefit from others must first consider how they might benefit them.

He continued, "Since the beginning of successive dynasties, including the time of the August Emperor (Gao Huangdi), imperial edicts have been issued granting various monasteries stipends ranging from three thousand to five thousand [coins], with the minimum being three hundred to five hundred."
The Sangha shall have no anxiety regarding a lack of food. Once the formal decree has been entered within the monastic community, they shall enjoy lifelong exemption from corvée labor.

Government officials shall treat them as honored guests. At all passes and ferries, they may not be obstructed or detained. Should any commoner humiliate or insult them, the punishment shall be light whipping for minor offenses and the amputation of hands for grave ones.
As for all their lands and property, the law does not permit them to be sold, nor does it permit them to be purchased. Both the giver and the receiver [shall incur penalty].
This is a transgression. Those who use force to encroach upon and seize property are as recorded in the Imperial Archives.

The reason people formerly delighted in becoming ordained monks was, fundamentally, because there were material benefits to be gained. Now it is no longer so: agricultural lands are seized by the powerful and influential, yet the government does not investigate;
monks are insulted by laypeople, yet the government does not protect them. Consequently, their assets are exhausted and their temples fall into ruin.

Relying on solicited alms to pass the days, what need is there for an internal decree? If one possesses newly acquired property from secular sources—where there are fields subject to labor service and people subject to the household register—one is originally no different from the common people; why then would an internal decree be required?

Furthermore, after receiving an internal decree, one must pray for fine weather, request rain, assemble rituals, worship at spirit tablets, welcome officials, and receive the provincial authorities, which only increases one's burdens. Should one fail to appear when summoned by name, then...

The punishment is the same as for those who hold official emoluments (*yù*). [The registers] list twenty-eight ancestral generations. If one is humiliated by a layperson, it is no different from being treated like a pig or a dog;
how could one then claim to be among those with official emoluments? According to the law, one should not be subjected to such humiliation. In what way does this differ from a commoner?
Beyond the mandatory corvée labor, why must there be an additional internal register (*nèi-dié*)? Alas! The records of the Venerable Founder (*Gāohuángdì*) still exist. The Venerable Founder...
The Sage’s intent was never carried out. Since it brought no benefit to the monks, it is no wonder that they were unwilling to accept the internal edict.
*Kaiguroku* (End).
